## Why Project Management Matters

A consistent project structure means a collaborator — or you, six months from now — can open your folder and immediately understand what goes where, without asking you a single question. This is one piece of what we mean by **[reproducibility](/glossary.qmd#reproducibility)**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-live"></span> Try It Live — No Local R? Read This First
The folder structure, `renv`, and README steps below require a persistent
filesystem — something a browser sandbox can't provide. Directories
created in webR exist only for this page session and disappear on
refresh.

Read through these steps to understand *why* a reproducible project needs
them, but you'll need a local R install (Positron or RStudio) to actually
build and keep a project folder. The dataset-loading steps further down
*do* work live in your browser, in a dedicated Try It Live block, since
they don't depend on anything being saved.
:::

## Create an R Project

In Positron: **File → New Folder from Project Template → [R Project](/glossary.qmd#r-project)**, or create a plain folder and open it in Positron as your working directory.

## Build Your Folder Structure

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create("raw_data")
dir.create("processed_data")
dir.create("scripts")
dir.create("outputs")
```

| Folder | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `raw_data/` | Original data. Never edit these files directly. |
| `processed_data/` | Cleaned, transformed versions of your data. |
| `scripts/` | Your code. |
| `outputs/` | Figures, tables, and results. |

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tour"></span> Code Tour — File Naming Conventions
- No spaces — use `_` or `-` instead
- Start timestamped files with an ISO date: `YYYY-MM-DD`
- Be descriptive

**Avoid:**
- ❌ `data analysis.R` (spaces)
- ❌ `data.csv` (not descriptive)
- ❌ `final_FINAL_really_final.R` (version chaos)

**Prefer:**
- ✅ `2024-03-15_survey_analysis.R`
- ✅ `participant_demographics_clean.csv`
- ✅ `README.md`
:::

## What Is a Package?

Base R ships with a core set of built-in functions. A **package** is an
add-on that extends what R can do — installed once per machine with
`install.packages()`, then turned on for each new R session with
`library()`. The very next tool we use, `renv`, is a package — and it
needs to be installed before it can do anything.

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("renv")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Minimal Packages, On Purpose
This series installs very few packages before Arc 5. That's deliberate:
the goal here is understanding what a package actually *does* for you —
`renv` protects reproducibility, `fs` generates a file tree — not
accumulating a long list of dependencies before you've seen why any one
of them earns its place.
:::

## Initialize `renv`

[renv](/glossary.qmd#renv) tracks exactly which package versions your project uses, so it runs the same way on any machine, including yours a year from now.

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::init()
renv::snapshot()
```

This creates:

```
├── .Rprofile
├── renv.lock
└── renv/
    ├── .gitignore
    ├── activate.R
    ├── settings.json
    └── library/
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — What's Actually Inside renv.lock?
```json
{
  "R": { "Version": "4.6.0" },
  "Packages": {
    "dplyr": {
      "Package": "dplyr",
      "Version": "1.1.4",
      "Source": "Repository"
    }
  }
}
```
Every package your project depends on gets pinned to an exact version
here. When a collaborator runs `renv::restore()`, R installs these exact
versions — not whatever happens to be newest that day. Full documentation
is at [rstudio.github.io/renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/).
:::

## Load the Dataset

We'll use this dataset — real RNA-seq data from a published Shank3 mouse
study — for the rest of the series. Two files: a raw counts matrix, and a
metadata file describing each sample. We'll call them `raw_data` and
`raw_metadata` throughout, matching the `raw_data/` folder they live in.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# ---- Download once, save locally ----
metadata_url  <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv"
rawcounts_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv"

download.file(metadata_url,  destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
download.file(rawcounts_url, destfile = "raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")

raw_metadata <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
raw_data     <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")
```

Inspect what you loaded:

```{r}
#| eval: false
head(raw_metadata)
str(raw_metadata)
dim(raw_data)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Why Download-and-Save Here, but Read-from-URL Below?
This isn't an inconsistency — it's intentional. In a real project, raw
data should live inside your project folder (`raw_data/`) so your
analysis doesn't silently depend on the internet being available every
time you run it. If the GitHub repo moves, is renamed, or GitHub has an
outage, a project with a local copy still runs. A project that re-fetches
a URL every time does not.

Browser-based tools like webR can't save a persistent local copy the way
a laptop can, so reading from the URL each time is the necessary
workaround for that environment — not the ideal pattern. You're seeing a
real technical tradeoff, not a mistake.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-live"></span> Try It Live — Load the Real Dataset in Your Browser
No local file system here, so these read directly from the source URL
instead of a saved copy — see the About This box above for why that's a
tradeoff, not the ideal pattern.

```{webr-r}
raw_metadata <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv")
head(raw_metadata)
```

```{webr-r}
raw_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CWML/ARCS/main/data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")
dim(raw_data)
```
:::

## Write a [README](/glossary.qmd#readme)

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("fs")
library(fs)
fs::dir_tree()
capture.output(fs::dir_tree(), file = "README.txt")
```

Then open `README.txt` and fill in the template:

```
This readme file was generated on [YYYY-MM-DD] by [NAME]

GENERAL INFORMATION

Title of Dataset:

Author/Principal Investigator Information
Name:
ORCID:
Institution:
Address:
Email:

SHARING/ACCESS INFORMATION

This data was retrieved through the GREIN web platform, which
interfaces with the NIH Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository.
Link to dataset: https://www.ilincs.org/apps/grein/?gse=GSE113754

DATA & FILE OVERVIEW

raw_data/        — original data (never edited)
processed_data/  — cleaned data
scripts/         — analysis code
outputs/         — figures, tables, results
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — README Templates
This project's README is a simplified version of the Cornell Research
Data Management README template: [Cornell eCommons README Template](https://ecommons.cornell.edu/entities/publication/6effe964-798e-4c21-aac2-4194709ff230)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — The Project Is the Unit of Reproducibility
It's tempting to think of a single script as "the analysis." But a script
alone can't be reproduced — it depends on data files, package versions,
and a folder structure that has to exist for it to run. The **project**,
not the script, is what makes your work reproducible: the folders, the
`renv.lock`, the raw data, and the code together. If you zipped your
project folder and sent it to a stranger, could they run it? That's the
real test.
:::

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** a reproducible project with a standard folder
structure, `renv` tracking this project's exact dependencies, a real
genomics dataset (`raw_data` and `raw_metadata`) loaded and inspected,
and a README documenting all of it.

**Why it matters:** think about the future as you form these habits —
document and automate iteratively, give your work collaborative
potential — so reproducibility becomes how you work, not a checklist
someone hands you afterward.
